name: Non-Technical
description: Business, marketing, leadership, sales, communication, finance and management subjects.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.guidance: Hook the reader with the stake: what changes for them once they master this chapter. If the chapter centres on a concrete thing worth seeing (a model, a structure, a named framework), follow the opening paragraph with one well-labelled `image` block (`image_kind: diagram`) that orients the reader before any other section.

sections.label: Learning Objectives
sections.guidance: 3-6 outcome-focused objectives written in plain business language.

sections.label: Story / Scenario
sections.guidance: A short, believable scenario with a named role and a concrete situation. End with the takeaway it sets up.

sections.label: Core Concept
sections.guidance: Explain the idea in plain language, then define any jargon you must introduce. If the concept has parts, stages or a relationship worth seeing, add an `image` block with `image_kind: diagram` (smart_art or conceptual work well here) instead of only describing it in prose.

sections.label: Real-World Example
sections.guidance: A recognisable example. Only name real companies or figures when the research supports it.

sections.label: Case Study
sections.guidance: Context, challenge, actions taken, outcome, lessons. Keep it honest - include what did not work.

sections.label: Framework / Method
sections.guidance: Give the reader a repeatable model or checklist they can apply on Monday morning. Whenever the framework has named steps, stages or a 2x2/quadrant shape, add an `image` block with `image_kind: diagram` (flow_chart, cycle, hierarchy, comparison or smart_art - whichever fits) instead of only listing it as text.

sections.label: Practical Application
sections.guidance: Translate the framework into specific actions for the target audience's day-to-day work.

sections.label: Common Mistakes
sections.guidance: The traps people actually fall into, with the early warning sign for each.

sections.label: Pro Tips
sections.guidance: Insider advice that is specific and immediately usable.

sections.label: Reflection
sections.guidance: 2-4 questions that make the reader apply the chapter to their own context.

sections.label: Exercise
sections.guidance: A practical activity: a draft, a conversation plan, a worksheet, an audit of their own work.

sections.label: Quiz
sections.guidance: 3-5 scenario-based questions with answers and short explanations.

sections.label: Summary
sections.guidance: Key takeaways plus the bridge into the next chapter.

writer_guidance: Write in warm, confident, plain business English. Short sentences. Prefer a concrete story or example over abstract theory. Avoid buzzword stacking and motivational filler. Never invent statistics, quotes or company outcomes - use only what the research supports, and say 'often' rather than fabricating a number. Code blocks are rarely appropriate; use tables and checklists instead.
research_guidance: Prioritise reputable business sources: industry reports, established publications, documented company cases and peer-reviewed management research. Capture named examples, dated statistics with their source, and frameworks with their original author.
review_focus: practical relevance - can the reader act on this tomorrow
no fabricated statistics, quotes or company outcomes
story and example quality: specific rather than generic
jargon is defined before it is used
image_guidance: Prefer clean conceptual illustrations, framework diagrams or simple quadrant/matrix visuals on a light background. Flat modern vector style, minimal text, no stock-photo clichés, no photorealistic faces.

theme.font_family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
